analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal tax credit for donations to private-school scholarship funds to $1,700, doubled for married couples.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2026 with no cosponsors; the bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends a federal tax credit (Section 25F of the tax code) that lets taxpayers reduce their federal income tax bill, dollar for dollar, when they donate to scholarship-granting organizations that pay for children to attend private elementary and secondary schools. The bill would raise the maximum credit from $1,000 per person to $1,700, and from $2,000 to $3,400 for joint filers, and index the cap to inflation going forward. Because the credit is dollar-for-dollar and only offsets taxes actually owed, the biggest users are households with meaningful federal tax liability.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who donate to private-school scholarship organizations gain a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for larger gifts, and families who receive scholarships from those organizations gain more available tuition money. Private elementary and secondary schools gain a larger, inflation-protected pipeline of donated funding. The credit is nonrefundable, so the taxpayers best positioned to use it fully are those with enough income tax liability to absorb a $1,700 (or $3,400) credit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the maximum Section 25F scholarship tax credit to $1,700 per taxpayer, or $3,400 on a joint return, and adjusts the amount for inflation after 2026.

Section 25F is a nonrefundable federal tax credit for contributions to scholarship-granting organizations, which award scholarships covering elementary and secondary school tuition, generally at private schools; general knowledge of how the existing credit works, with the amended dollar limits and inflation adjustment specified in the bill text.
The change applies retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through forgone federal income tax revenue. Every dollar of credit claimed is a dollar the Treasury does not collect, and those forgone dollars are directed by donors to private-school scholarship organizations rather than to general federal purposes.

drawbacks.text: The credit is nonrefundable, meaning a taxpayer gets no benefit beyond the taxes they already owe; households with little or no federal income tax liability cannot use it, so the direct tax benefit flows to taxpayers with higher incomes even if the scholarships themselves can go to lower-income students.
The expansion costs the Treasury forgone revenue, with the money directed by individual donors toward private-school tuition rather than being available for public purposes.
The bill does not change how scholarship-granting organizations select recipients or account for their spending; it only enlarges the amount of tax- subsidized money flowing through them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real benefit to families who use private-school scholarships and to the donors who fund them, at a real cost to the Treasury. Its main design weakness is that the credit itself is most valuable to taxpayers who owe substantial income tax, so the direct tax benefit tilts toward higher-income donors even where the scholarship money may reach lower-income students. It is a modest, incremental expansion of an existing program rather than a large transfer, but it entrenches the scholarship-organization pipeline as the channel for tax-subsidized K-12 education funding.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the final months of the session and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Hyde-Smith introduced S. 5322 on August 6, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No senators have signed on as cosponsors.
The action history shows no steps beyond introduction and committee referral, with no markup, hearing, or floor vote listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: the bill has drawn no cosponsors and no committee action, so current law remains unchanged and the outcome is simply that the bill sits untouched in committee as the session winds down.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits untouched

for.name: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from Mississippi and bill sponsor

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator introduced the bill and no other senator, from either party, signed on as a cosponsor; no votes have occurred.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools and scholarship-granting organizations
industries.note: The bill enlarges the dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for donations to scholarship-granting organizations, locking in these organizations as the permanent channel for tax-subsidized private-school tuition money. Some families gain scholarship funds toward private school, but the tax subsidy flows through donor-directed private institutions rather than public schools, and the tax benefit itself is most usable by higher-income donors.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has zero cosponsors and no committee action weeks after introduction, late in a Congress that ends January 3, 2027. Bills that reach this point without cosponsors or a scheduled markup almost never advance; the realistic path is that the bill expires quietly when the session ends, unless a companion vehicle picks up the provision elsewhere.
